en: Majjhima Nikāya 152:
The Discourse on the Development of the Faculties Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Gajaṅgalā in the Suveḷu Grove.
Then the young brahmin Uttara, a pupil of Pārāsariya, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As the young brahmin Uttara, pupil of Pārāsariya, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Uttara, does the brahmin Pārāsīviya teach his disciples the development of the faculties?
“He does, Master Gotama; the brahmin Pārāsīviya teaches his disciples the development of the faculties.
“But how, Uttara, does the brahmin Pārāsīviya teach his disciples the development of the faculties?”
“Here, Master Gotama, one does not see a form with the eye, nor does one hear a sound with the ear— it is in this way, Master Gotama,
that the brahmin Pārāsīya teaches the cultivation of the faculties to his disciples.
“If that were so, Uttara, then a blind man would have cultivated faculties, and a deaf man would have cultivated faculties.”
"Just as was the word of the brahmin Pārāsiviya:
'For a blind man, Uttara, does not see a form with his eye; a deaf man does not hear a sound with his ear.
When this was said, the young brahmin Uttara, the pupil of Pārāsiviya, sat silent, abashed, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, brooding, and speechless.

Then the Blessed One, having understood that the young brahmin Uttara, a pupil of Pārāsariya, was silent, abashed, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, brooding, and speechless, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“Ānanda, the brahmin Pārāsariya teaches the development of the faculties to his disciples in one way, but in the Noble One’s discipline, Ānanda, the unsurpassed development of the faculties is quite another.
“This is the time for this, Blessed One; this is the time for this, Sugata.”
“May the Blessed One teach the unsurpassed development of the faculties in the Noble One’s Discipline. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, Ānanda, listen and attend closely;
I shall speak,” said the Blessed One. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And how, Ānanda, is there the unsurpassed development of the faculties in the discipline of the Noble Ones?
Here, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.”
Thus he understands:
“This agreeable [feeling] has arisen in me; this disagreeable [feeling] has arisen in me; this both agreeable and disagreeable [feeling] has arisen in me.
And yet, it is conditioned, gross, dependently arisen.”
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely equanimity. Thus,
whatever pleasant feeling has arisen, whatever unpleasant feeling has arisen, and whatever neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling has arisen, all cease within him.
Equanimity becomes established.
Just as, Ānanda, a person with good eyesight might open his eyes after closing them, or close his eyes after opening them;
even so, Ānanda, for whomever pleasant, unpleasant, or both pleasant and unpleasant feelings that have arisen cease so quickly, so swiftly, and so effortlessly, equanimity becomes established.
This, Ānanda, is called the unsurpassed development of the faculties regarding forms cognizable by the eye in the discipline of the Noble One.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu hears a sound with the ear, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
He understands thus:
‘This agreeable [feeling] has arisen in me; this disagreeable [feeling] has arisen in me; this both agreeable and disagreeable feeling has arisen in me.
And yet, it is conditioned, gross, dependently arisen.
This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely:’
‘Equanimity.
For him, whatever pleasant feeling has arisen, whatever unpleasant feeling has arisen, and whatever neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling has arisen, cease;
equanimity becomes established.
"Just as, Ānanda, a strong man might snap his fingers with ease,
even so, Ānanda, for whosoever pleasant, unpleasant, or both pleasant and unpleasant feelings that have arisen cease so quickly, so swiftly, so easily, and equanimity is established— this, Ānanda,
is called the unsurpassed development of the faculties regarding sounds cognizable by the ear in the discipline of the Noble One."
Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has smelled an odor with the nose, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
He understands thus:
‘This agreeable has arisen in me; this disagreeable has arisen; this both agreeable and disagreeable has arisen.’
And yet that is conditioned, gross, and dependently arisen.
This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely:
equanimity.”
Whatever pleasant feeling arises in him, whatever unpleasant feeling arises, and whatever neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling arises, it ceases;
equanimity becomes established.
Just as, Ānanda, when a lotus leaf is slightly tilted, drops of water roll off and do not remain settled;

In the same way, Ānanda, for whomever pleasant, unpleasant, or both pleasant and unpleasant feelings that have arisen cease so swiftly, so quickly, and with such ease, and equanimity is established— this, Ānanda,
is called the unsurpassed development of the faculties regarding odors cognizable by the nose in the discipline of the Noble One.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has tasted a flavor with the tongue, a pleasant feeling arises, an unpleasant feeling arises, or a feeling that is both pleasant and unpleasant arises.
Thus he understands:
"This agreeable has arisen for me; this disagreeable has arisen; this both agreeable and disagreeable has arisen.
And yet, it is conditioned, gross, and dependently originated."
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely equanimity. Thus,
whatever pleasant feeling has arisen, whatever unpleasant feeling has arisen, and whatever neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling has arisen, all cease within him.
Equanimity becomes established. Just as, Ānanda,
a strong man might gather a lump of spittle on the tip of his tongue and spit it out with ease,
even so, Ānanda, for whomever pleasant, unpleasant, or both pleasant and unpleasant feelings that have arisen cease so quickly, so swiftly, and so easily, equanimity becomes established.
This, Ānanda, is called the unsurpassed development of the faculties regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue in the discipline of the Noble One.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has touched a tangible object with the body, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
He understands thus:
‘This agreeable [feeling] has arisen in me; this disagreeable [feeling] has arisen in me; this both agreeable and disagreeable feeling has arisen in me.
And yet, these are conditioned, gross, dependently arisen.
This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely—’
"Equanimity.
Thus, whatever pleasant feeling has arisen, whatever unpleasant feeling has arisen, and whatever neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling has arisen cease;
equanimity becomes established.
"Just as, Ānanda, a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,

even so, Ānanda, for whomever pleasant [feeling], unpleasant [feeling], or both pleasant and unpleasant [feeling] that have arisen cease so quickly, so rapidly, so effortlessly, and equanimity is established— this, Ānanda,
is called the unsurpassed development of the faculties regarding tactile objects cognizable by the body in the discipline of the Noble One."

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
He understands thus:
‘This agreeable has arisen in me; this disagreeable has arisen; this both agreeable and disagreeable has arisen.’
"And yet that is conditioned, gross, and dependently arisen.
This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely:
equanimity."
Whatever pleasant feeling has arisen in him, whatever unpleasant feeling has arisen, and whatever neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling has arisen, all cease;
equanimity becomes established.
Ānanda, it is just as if a strong man were to drop two or three drops of water into an iron cauldron heated throughout the day.
“Slow, Ānanda, is the falling of drops of water, yet they would quickly reach exhaustion and disappearance;

even so, Ānanda, for whomever pleasant, unpleasant, or both pleasant and unpleasant feelings that have arisen cease with such speed, such swiftness, and such ease, and equanimity becomes established— this, Ānanda,
is called the unsurpassed development of the faculties regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind in the discipline of the Noble One.”
In this way, Ānanda, there is the unsurpassed development of the faculties in the discipline of the Noble One.
And how, Ānanda, is one a trainee practicing the path?
Here, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
Thus, because of that pleasant [object] arisen, that unpleasant [object] arisen, and that both pleasant and unpleasant [object] arisen, one is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
Thus, because of that which has arisen as pleasant, that which has arisen as unpleasant, and that which has arisen as both pleasant and unpleasant, he is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted.
In this way, Ānanda, one is a trainee practicing the path.
And how, Ānanda, is one a noble one whose faculties are cultivated?
In this case, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
If he should wish: "May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive," he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive.
If he should wish: "May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive," he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, having set aside both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,” he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has heard a sound with the ear … [and so on] … has smelled an odor with the nose … has tasted a flavor with the tongue … [and so on] …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
If he so desires: "May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive," he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the non-repulsive and the repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” then he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending.
In this way, Ānanda, one is noble, with faculties developed.

Thus, Ānanda, in the discipline of the Noble One, the unsurpassed development of the faculties has been taught by me; the trainee practicing the path has been taught; and the noble one with developed faculties has been taught.
“Whatever, Ānanda, should have been done by a Teacher who seeks the welfare of his disciples and has compassion for them, out of compassion—that has been done by me for you.
Here, Ānanda, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda; do not be negligent, lest you later feel regret. This is my instruction to you.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, uplifted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The tenth discourse, “The Development of the Faculties,” is concluded.
The fifth chapter, “The Six Sense Bases,” is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Anāthapiṇḍika, Channa,
Puṇṇa, Nanda, Karāhu, and Rāhula.
The Sixfold Set, the Six Sense Bases,
the Purity of the City of Vindā,
and also the Cultivation of the Faculties.
The section has "Instruction" as its fifth.
This is the summary (uddāna) of the sections:
Devadaha, Anupada, and so forth.
The "Analysis of Emptiness" and the "Six Sense Bases":
these chapters are situated in the *Upari-pannāsaka*.
The *Upari-panṇāsaka* (The Final Fifty) is completed.
Adorned with three fifties,
the entire *Majjhima-nikāya* is finished.
